extracted.intended_audience: landscape painters, art students, and critics
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and critical principles for selecting, observing, and representing landscape: prioritising form, light and shade, historical truth, and sincere motive over mere colour effects or deceptive finish. Guidance applies to composition, execution, and the moral/evaluative judgment of works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color depends on association
rubrics_metrics.description: A color, in association with other colors, is different from the same color seen by itself. It has a distinct and peculiar power upon the retina dependent on its association.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe that local color is altered by adjacent colors and reflected light; do not treat color as an absolute property of an object. Example: the stones and gravel take green reflections from boughs; polished surfaces reflect sky or sun. Anti-pattern: painting local color as if it were fixed and independent of surroundings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncertainty whether two people see the same color
rubrics_metrics.description: It is totally impossible to prove that one man sees in the same thing the same color that another does though he may use the same name for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise the vagueness and subjectivity of color perception; this undercuts color's claim to be a defining characteristic of bodies. Practical consequence: color disagreements need not invalidate critique of a painting's color if the effect is consistent for the artist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color is not a primary characteristic of bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: The color of any object is not more dependent upon the nature of the object itself, and the eye beholding it, than on the color of the objects near it; in this respect also, therefore, it is no characteristic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let local color override more stable indicators of object identity. Prioritise other truthful means of representation (form, light) over exact hue matching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form includes outline and chiaroscuro
rubrics_metrics.description: Painters have a most inaccurate and careless habit of confining the term [form] to the outline of bodies, whereas it necessarily implies light and shade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing form, always consider the unity of outline with light and shade (chiaroscuro). The eye cannot know form without its chiaroscuro; therefore study both outline and modelling together rather than treating outline alone as form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of light and shade in conveying character
rubrics_metrics.description: The form, as told by light and shade, is always decided and evident, and the source of the chief character of every object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use chiaroscuro to express the chief character and identity of objects; atmospheric and reflected color often confuse local color, but light-and-shade relations remain stable. Priority: secure form/chiaroscuro before worrying about precise tones of color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical truths are most valuable
rubrics_metrics.description: Those [truths] are always most valuable which are most historical, that is, which tell us most about the past and future states of the object to which they belong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select facts that indicate growth, history, and likely future states (e.g., a tree's growth and energy) rather than transient stains or ephemeral details. Historical/truthful marks (strata, erosion) are more informative than changeable surface tints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form (specific form) is first of all truths; tone/light/color secondary
rubrics_metrics.description: The truths of specific form are the first and most important of all; and next to them, those truths of chiaroscuro... Altogether lower than these ... stand all effects of chiaroscuro which are productive merely of imitations of light and tone, and all effects of color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim first to communicate specific form (structure, proportions), then correct modelling (chiaroscuro); color effects and tone imitations should follow, not supersede, these priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deceptive chiaroscuro (solidity/projection) is lowest truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Those particular accuracies or tricks of chiaroscuro which cause objects to look projecting from the canvas... are not worthy of the name of truths... they require for their attainment the sacrifice of all others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid trading overall truth and relations for isolated tricks that make one object 'project' unnaturally. Such effects are jugglery that deceive but neither instruct nor exalt—useful only if they don't sacrifice essential relations in the picture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of facts depends on aim: imitation vs truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Painters range into two great classes; one aiming at the development of the exquisite truths of specific form, refined color, and ethereal space... and the other casting all these aside, to attain those particular truths of tone and chiaroscuro, which may trick the spectator into a belief of reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide your aim before selecting facts: are you conveying the essential truth and feeling of nature, or merely producing deceptive imitation? Choices of detail, color, and finish should follow that aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware valuing art merely for deception (old masters' imitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The great body of the old landscape painters... the deception of the senses was the great and first end of all their art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique works that aim chiefly at deceiving the untaught eye: they may show mastery of effect but often sacrifice beauty and essential truth. Example anti-patterns: over-detailed foregrounds designed only to 'trick' recognition; emphasis on relief against sky while ignoring anatomy of foliage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern painters: seek what is most important to tell
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern landscape painters... think only of conveying the impression of nature into the mind of the spectator... a greater sum of valuable, essential, and impressive truth in the works of two or three of our leading modern landscape painters, than in those of all the old masters put together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the modern aim of selecting and communicating the most important truths of a scene (form, space, feeling) rather than slavish imitation of recognisable details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art must show love, earnestness, and humility
rubrics_metrics.description: There is one thing wanting in all the doing of these men, and that is the very virtue by which the work of human mind chiefly rises above that of the Daguerreotype... Love: There is no evidence of their ever having gone to nature with any thirst, or received from her such emotion as could make them... lose sight of themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sincerity of feeling (love of nature) is essential: technique without love leads to cold, conventional work. Criterion for judgment: does the work show honest emotion and a record of personal engagement with nature?

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate whether a work adds to the 'chain of truth'
rubrics_metrics.description: Inquire respecting every work of art... whether it have any virtue or substance as a link in this chain of truth, whether it have recorded or interpreted anything before unknown, whether it have added one single stone to our heaven-pointing pyramid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge works by their contribution to knowledge, feeling, or truthful representation of nature; even small honest contributions are valuable. Reject works that add nothing new or sincere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject works motivated by vanity, idleness, or mere dexterity
rubrics_metrics.description: If... there be neither purpose nor fidelity in what is done, if it be an envious or powerless imitation... or a display of mere manual dexterity... Cast it out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motive matters: finish or skill for its own sake, or derivative imitation without purpose, renders a work worthless and even 'perilous.' In evaluation, consider the artist's motive and fidelity, not technique alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finish is virtuous only when it signifies passion or thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Both finish and impetuosity... may be the signs of passion, or of its reverse... Both the finish and incompletion are right where they are the signs of passion or of thought, and both are wrong... when they cease to be so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use finish where it expresses love and observation; avoid finish purely to show dexterity. Conversely, leave things unfinished if that incompletion is a truthful sign of intent or feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right concealment equals right exhibition; know when to omit
rubrics_metrics.description: There is as much finish in the right concealment of things as in the right exhibition of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceal or simplify details intentionally when nature conceals them (mist, space, light); do not insist on filling every area with the same level of detail. Priority of effects may demand leaving parts less worked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority rule: paint mist/space/light even if nothing else is exact
rubrics_metrics.description: To paint mist rightly, space rightly, and light rightly, it may be often necessary to paint nothing else rightly, but the rule is simple for all that; if the artist is painting something that he knows and loves... he is all right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the principal aim is atmosphere or light, focus on those elements even at the expense of precise detail elsewhere. The central truth of the picture should guide what is rendered accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value faithful, affectionate detail where appropriate (religious schools)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the perfect treatment of details of this kind, treatment as delicate and affectionate as it is elevated and manly, it is to the works of these schools alone that we can refer... the rose, the myrtle, and the lily... have received their fairest portraiture where they bear a sacred character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where detail serves meaning (foreground plants, sacred contexts), study and render them with loving fidelity; these truthful small details can be of great instructive and emotional value. Anti-pattern: neglecting foreground character (as in some English painters) harms the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious of conventionality in celebrated models
rubrics_metrics.description: The landscape of the Venetians was without effect on any contemporary in subsequent schools... the whole field of what they have done is so narrow, and therein is so much of what is only relatively right, and in itself false or imperfect, that the young and inexperienced painter could run no greater risk than the too early taking them for teachers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not adopt a master's conventional devices wholesale; test conventions against nature and the aims of your work. Examples: Venetian skies and foliage are powerful but narrow models—use with discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study sky and atmospheric gradation carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: His landscape is remarkable for the absolute truth of its sky, whose blue... is gradated to the horizon with a cautiousness and finish almost inconceivable; ... there is a wreath of rain cloud of warmer color floating above the mountains, lighted on its under edge, whose faithfulness to nature... is altogether exemplary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sky and atmosphere are crucial elements in landscape; study gradation, horizon light, and the play of cloud light and shadow. Use careful observation and subtle gradation rather than theatrical color.
